en: The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Radiance of Supreme Excellence, adorned with the seven precious gems.
Majestic, it emits a great radiance that universally illumines all boundless worlds.

Immeasurable regions are exquisitely adorned and arranged in a circular expanse without limit; its magnitude is difficult to fathom, surpassing the spheres traversed by the three realms, arising from supramundane roots of goodness, and characterized by the most supreme sovereignty of pure consciousness.

It is the capital where the Tathāgata resides, where the assembly of great Bodhisattvas gathers like clouds, and where immeasurable devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans constantly attend as his retinue. Sustained by the joy and bliss of the vast Dharma-flavor, it accomplishes every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings, extinguishing the crosswise entanglements and defilements of all afflictions, remaining far removed from all Māras, and transcending all [worldly] adornments.

It is the locus upon which the Tathāgatas rely for their adornment; it takes great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct as its pathways; it takes great tranquility and sublime insight as its vehicle; it takes the gateways of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as its points of entry; it is adorned by a multitude of immeasurable merits, and it is established by a multitude of great jewel-flower kings.

Within that great palace, this Bhagavat possesses the most purified awakening; he manifests non-duality, proceeds toward the signless dharma, abides in the Buddha-abode, has attained the equality of all Buddhas, reached the state of non-obstruction, and his unshakeable activity is unhindered.

That which is established is inconceivable; they roam within the equal dharma-nature of the three periods of time; their bodies are distributed throughout all worlds; regarding all dharmas, their wisdom is free from doubt or obstruction; regarding all practices, they have achieved great awakening; regarding the wisdom of all dharmas, they possess no uncertainty; whatever bodies they manifest cannot be conceptually differentiated; they possess the very wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas; they have attained the Buddha’s non-dual dwelling on the supreme other shore, remaining unmixed with others.

The Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom of liberation is ultimate; he has realized the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is without middle or limit, reaching the furthest extent of the dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of space, and extending to the end of the future.

Together with a great assembly of immeasurable *śrāvakas*—all of whom were disciplined and compliant, true sons of the Buddha, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated, whose precepts were perfectly pure, who sought the joy of the Dharma, and who had heard much and retained what they had heard;
whose hearing had accumulated, who were skilled in reflecting upon what they reflected upon, skilled in speaking what they spoke, and skilled in performing what they performed;
and who possessed swift wisdom, rapid wisdom, sharp wisdom, emerging wisdom, superior discerning wisdom, great wisdom, and vast wisdom.

Possessing peerless wisdom, accomplished in the treasure of insight, endowed with the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*), they have attained the foremost dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
They are a great and pure field of merit, their deportment is tranquil, and they are fully accomplished in great patience and gentleness without decline.
Having well practiced the holy teachings of the Tathāgata—there were also immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [of this kind].
The Bodhisattvas, having come together from all Buddha-fields— each abiding in the Great Vehicle and traversing the path of the Great Vehicle,
with minds impartial toward all sentient beings, free from all conceptualization, non-conceptualization, and manifold discrimination, having crushed all Māras and adversaries,
and being far removed from all attachments and mental preoccupations characteristic of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— [gathered there].
They were distinct, sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Dharma, transcending the five fears,
and resolutely entering the stage of non-retrogression; they stood before them on the ground where all the afflictions and oppressions of sentient beings are stilled—
headed by the Bodhisattva Wonderful Birth (Sujāta).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Maitreya, you should know that there are five kinds of dharmas that encompass the stage of Great Enlightenment. What are these five?"
These are the so-called pure dharma-realm, the great mirror-like wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

"Wondrous Birth, you should know that the pure dharma-realm is like space: although it pervades all various forms and diverse characteristics, it cannot be said to possess those various characteristics; its essence is of a single flavor."

In this way, although the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm pervades all various categories of knowable objects, it cannot be said to possess various characteristics, for its essence is of a single flavor.
"Furthermore, just as space, though pervading all forms, is never separated from them, yet is not defiled by the faults of those forms;
so too the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, though pervading the mental nature of all sentient beings, is never separated from it due to its reality, yet is not defiled by their faults."
"Furthermore, just as space contains all actions of body, speech, and mind, yet this space has no activity or effort,
so too does the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm contain all the deeds manifested by omniscience for the benefit of sentient beings, while the pure dharma-realm itself has no activity or effort."
“Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances manifest arising and ceasing within space, yet this space itself has neither arising nor ceasing;

so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the manifestations of the transformations of wisdom that benefit sentient beings appear to arise and cease, yet the pure dharma-realm has neither arising nor ceasing.”
"Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances manifest as increasing or decreasing within space, yet this space neither increases nor decreases;

so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s nectar-like holy teaching appears to increase or decrease, yet the pure dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases."

"Furthermore, just as the forms and appearances in the ten directions within space are boundless and inexhaustible because the realm of space itself is boundless and inexhaustible, yet this space neither goes nor comes, and neither moves nor turns."

Thus, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the establishment of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions involves various activities that are boundless and inexhaustible, because the pure dharma-realm is itself boundless and inexhaustible; yet, this pure dharma-realm neither comes nor goes, and it is without movement or transformation.
"Furthermore, just as within space the trichiliocosm appears to be destroyed and appears to be formed, yet the realm of space itself neither undergoes destruction nor formation;

so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, immeasurable signs appear as the attainment of perfect enlightenment, or again, the manifestation of entry into great parinirvāṇa, yet the pure dharma-realm neither attains perfect enlightenment nor enters into cessation."

"Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances—such as decay, putrefaction, burning, and drying out—are observed to undergo transformation in dependence upon space, yet the realm of space is not transformed by them nor does it suffer weariness or exhaustion."

Thus, within the realm of sentient beings that relies upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm, various violations of the precepts regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind may be found; yet the pure dharma-realm does not undergo transformation because of them, nor does it suffer any weariness or exhaustion.

"Furthermore, just as the earth, great mountains, light, water, fire, Śakra, his retinue, and even the various phenomena of the sun and moon are all perceivable by depending upon space, yet the realm of space is not any of those characteristics."

In this way, based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm, the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation can be found; yet the pure dharma-realm is not those various characteristics.

"Furthermore, just as within space various causes and conditions arise in succession, such that the revolving cycle of immeasurable worlds in the trichiliocosm can be perceived, yet the realm of space itself performs no act of arising."

Thus, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the circular assemblies of all Buddhas endowed with immeasurable marks can be perceived, yet the pure dharma-realm itself is devoid of any arising or activity.
"Furthermore, Wondrous Birth!
As for the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, it is like the manifestation of various images and reflections depending upon a round mirror.
In the same way, depending upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror, the various images of the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses manifest."

As for using the circular mirror as a metaphor alone, one should know that the circular mirror and the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror are equal and identical; therefore, the wisdom-mirror is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

"Just as when a person seeking merit and happiness hangs a great round mirror in a high and excellent place so that it remains unshaken, immeasurable sentient beings coming and going observe their own virtues and faults therein, desiring to preserve their virtues and abandon all faults."

In this way, the Tathāgata suspends the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom within the pure *dharmadhātu*; because it is uninterrupted, it is unshakable. This is intended so that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings may contemplate both defilement and purity, desiring to adopt the pure and abandon all that is defiled.
"Furthermore, just as a perfectly polished, round mirror is clear, stainless, and its radiance shines everywhere, so too is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Because it has forever transcended the stains of all afflictive and cognitive hindrances (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the Buddha-wisdom, it is perfectly polished; because it is sustained by the meditative concentration that serves as its support, it is clear and stainless; and because it performs the work of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, its radiance shines everywhere."
"Furthermore, just as various reflected images and appearances arise depending upon the fundamental object (bimba) in relation to a round mirror,
so too do various images of wisdom and their appearances arise at all times in the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata, depending upon various conditions."
"Just as numerous images arise upon a circular mirror, yet there are no images upon that circular mirror, and this circular mirror is without movement or activity."

In this way, upon the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the reflections of many diverse cognitions arise; yet, although these reflections of various cognitions appear upon the mirror-like wisdom, that wisdom-mirror is itself without movement or activity.
"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is neither joined with nor separated from its various reflected images— because it does not aggregate them, yet manifests them through conditions—
so too is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom neither joined with nor separated from the reflections of various wisdoms, because it does not aggregate them, yet does not lose them."

"Furthermore, just as a perfectly polished round mirror serves as the pervasive basis and condition for the arising of all reflected images in every place, so too does the Great Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata—constantly and flawlessly polished by immeasurable virtuous practices—serve as the pervasive basis and condition for the arising of all images of wisdom.

These include the images of wisdom of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the images of wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the images of wisdom of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. This is for the sake of enabling those of the Śrāvaka vehicle to attain liberation by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle, those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle to attain liberation by relying on the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and those of the Mahāyāna to attain liberation by relying on the Unsurpassed Vehicle."

"Just as great reflections can be perceived within a round mirror—namely, the reflections of the great earth, great mountains, great trees, and great palaces—yet that round mirror is not equal in size to those objects."

Thus, upon the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), the reflections of wisdom from the Stage of Utmost Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) up to the Buddha-stage can be perceived, as well as the reflections of all mundane and supramundane phenomena; yet the mirror-like wisdom itself is not limited by their measure.

"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is not the condition for the arising of reflections from objects that are obstructed, so too the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the Tathāgata is not the condition for the arising of the cognitive images of sentient beings who are hindered by being under the influence of evil friends or by hearing incorrect teachings; for they are not suitable vessels."
"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is not a condition for the arising of reflections from objects situated in darkness,

so too the Great Mirror-like Wisdom of the Tathāgata is not a condition for the arising of the reflection of wisdom in sentient beings who delight in evil and are shrouded in ignorance, because they are not suitable vessels."

"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is not a condition for the arising of images from objects located at a distance, so too the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the Tathāgata is not a condition for the arising of the images of wisdom in sentient beings who are impure, who have accumulated karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma, or who lack faith; for they are not suitable vessels."
"Furthermore, Wondrous Birth!
The wisdom of equality is fully accomplished through ten aspects.
It realizes the supreme joy of all marks because the equality of the dharma-nature is fully accomplished;..."
Because they have realized the equality of the nature of phenomena through the perfect fulfillment of all experiences of dependent origination;
because they have realized the equality of the nature of phenomena through the perfect fulfillment of being free from distinct characteristics and the absence of characteristics;
and because they have realized the equality of the nature of phenomena through the perfect fulfillment of great compassion that universally rescues and aids.
Because the perfection of the nature of equality is fully accomplished, there is great compassion that is independent;
because the perfection of the nature of equality is fully accomplished, he manifests according to the inclinations of all sentient beings;
because the perfection of the nature of equality is fully accomplished, all sentient beings respectfully receive what he teaches.
The world and tranquility are of one single flavor, because the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is perfectly fulfilled;
all phenomena of the world—suffering and pleasure—are of one single flavor, because the equal nature of phenomena is perfectly fulfilled;
the ultimate cultivation of immeasurable merit is perfected, because the equal nature of phenomena is perfectly fulfilled.
"Furthermore, Wondrous Birth!

As for the wisdom of wondrous observation, it is like the world-system that sustains the realm of sentient beings; in this same way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation sustains all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates, and provides unimpeded eloquent exposition of the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas."
"Furthermore, just as this world serves as the causal condition for all sentient beings to suddenly give rise to all manner of infinite consciousnesses of various characteristics,

so too does the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) serve as the causal condition for the sudden arising of all manner of infinite consciousnesses of various characteristics— the unimpeded, wondrous wisdom regarding all that is knowable."

"Furthermore, just as the world is delightful, adorned with various things to enjoy such as gardens, groves, and ponds, so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation delightful, being adorned with various things to enjoy:

the perfections (pāramitās), the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), the ten powers (daśabala), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma)."

"Furthermore, it is like the world, with its continents, islands, suns, moons, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heavens, all exquisitely adorned and arranged in succession."

Thus, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation—regarding the causes and effects of worldly and supramundane decline and prosperity, as well as the complete realization by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—is adorned with a flawless and exquisite array of observations.
"Furthermore, just as the world is for the vast enjoyment of all sentient beings,

so too does the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation manifest the assemblies of all Buddhas and rain down the great Dharma rain, in order to cause sentient beings to experience the great joy of the Dharma."
"Just as the five destinies are found within the world— namely, the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods— so too,
upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, the distinctions of the five destinies, with their boundless causes and effects, appear fully manifest."
"Just as the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are found within the world,
so too, upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, the infinite distinctions of the three realms, together with their causes and effects, are fully manifested."
"Just as the great king of mountains, Sumeru and others, can be perceived as manifesting within the world,
so too can the vast and profound teachings, brought forth by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, be perceived upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation."
"Just as in the world one may find a vast, profound, and unshakeable great ocean, so too,
upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, one may find the teaching of the profound *dharmadhātu*, which cannot be shaken by any celestial Māras, external paths, or heterodox arguments."
"Furthermore, just as the world is surrounded by the Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa),

so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) surrounded by all particular and universal characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa), without being deluded regarding them."
"Furthermore, O Subhūti!

As for the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), it is like the diligent physical activities of sentient beings; by means of these, sentient beings pursue various ends, such as seeking profit, engaging in agriculture, or laboring at their crafts."

In this way, through the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), he exerts himself in the transformative activity of the body; by means of this, the Tathāgata manifests in various fields of arts and crafts to subdue those beings who are arrogant regarding their skills. Through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.
"Furthermore, just as sentient beings experience bodily karma, by which they enjoy various objects such as forms and so forth;

likewise, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplished action experiences the karma of manifesting bodies, by which the Tathāgata goes to the various places of birth among sentient beings, manifesting birth as one of their own kind while dwelling in a position of honor.

Because he manifests birth as one of their own kind, he subdues all sentient beings of different kinds; through the power of such skillful means, he leads sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation."
"Furthermore, just as sentient beings experience bodily karma, and by means of this, sentient beings experience the fruits of the good and evil deeds they have performed;

so too does the Tathāgata’s Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done experience the karma of bodily emanations. By means of this, the Tathāgata manifests the experience of various difficult practices throughout his past lives and previous births. Through the power of such skillful means, he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation."

“Furthermore, just as sentient beings engage in the verbal karma of congratulation and consolation, whereby they converse with one another and offer mutual greetings and comfort, so too does the Tathāgata’s transformative activity of celebratory speech—arising from his *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done)—proclaim various teachings according to the inclinations of beings. These teachings are skillful in both phrasing and meaning; even sentient beings of small wisdom believe them upon first hearing.
By the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.”

"Furthermore, it is like the conventional verbal karma of sentient beings; by means of this, sentient beings instruct one another in succession, dedicating themselves to their respective tasks, condemning evil and praising good, and summoning one another."

In this way, through the transformative activity of speech arising from the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), the Tathāgata establishes the correct rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), censures all forms of negligence, and praises heedfulness.

Furthermore, they establish those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin); through the power of such skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they lead all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.
"Furthermore, just as sentient beings engage in the vocal activity of eloquent discourse, whereby they successively reveal and explain various treatises whose meanings are not yet understood;

so too does the Tathāgata, through the vocal transformative activity of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done, sever the immeasurable doubts of sentient beings. By means of this power of skillful expedient means, he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation."
“Furthermore, just as sentient beings exercise the karma of mental deliberation (*manas-karman*), by which they determine what is to be done and what is not to be done;

so too does the Tathāgata exercise the transformative karma of the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), by which he discerns the eighty-four thousand differences in the mental activities of sentient beings. Through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.”

"Furthermore, just as sentient beings perform mental karma, and by means of this they perform various kinds of karmic actions, so too does the Tathāgata perform the karma of mental transformation through his *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*.

By means of this, the Tathāgata observes the conduct of sentient beings—their practices and non-practices, their gains and losses—in order to cause them to adopt and abandon; he then performs remedial measures.
Through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation."
“Furthermore, just as sentient beings initiate mental karma, and by means of this, sentient beings initiate various [other] karmas;

so too does the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplished action initiate the karma of mental transformation. By means of this, because the Tathāgata desires to proclaim their antidotes, he manifests for them the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables that they delight in.
Through the power of such skillful means, he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.”

"Furthermore, just as sentient beings receive and experience mental karma, by which they undergo suffering and pleasure, so too does the Tathāgata’s *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done) receive and experience the karma of mental transformation.

By means of this, the Tathāgata provides definitive explanations through the four modes of answering—definitive, non-definitive, counter-questioning, and setting aside—and accordingly receives and understands the meanings of the past, future, and present.
Through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings into the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, is it only the Tathāgata who,
within the pure dharma-realm, enjoys the unified wisdom of the single flavor of phenomena, or can all bodhisattvas also do so?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
“They are also able to experience the wisdom of phenomena as a single, harmonious flavor.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the wisdom of the single-flavored activity that Bodhisattvas enjoy?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a Bodhisattva who has realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena attains the understanding of that patience within the state of non-arising phenomena, they counteract dualistic perceptions. By dispelling the two types of perception—self and other—they attain a mind of equality.”
"From this point onward, those bodhisattvas no longer manifest the conceptual distinction between self and others, and they partake in the wisdom of phenomena as a single, unified flavor.
The Bodhisattva Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the Tathāgata will extensively provide parables so that all bodhisattvas may realize this profound meaning, and so that it may be widely proclaimed and disseminated according to the needs of those to be converted, enabling all sentient beings to quickly awaken to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas upon hearing it."
The Buddha told Maitreya:

“For example, as long as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have not entered the Grove of Miscellaneous Delights (Miśrakavana), they are ultimately unable to enjoy objects or sensations in a manner that is free from the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine. Once they enter the Grove of Miscellaneous Delights, however, they enjoy them at will without any conceptual discrimination.”

Because this Grove of Miscellaneous Delights possesses such virtues, it enables all the devas who enter this grove to experience the various karmic fruits of the heavens—both their objects and their sensations—in a state of spontaneous harmony, without the need for deliberate thought.

In this way, if a bodhisattva has not yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they can never attain an equanimous mind or equanimous relinquishment; they remain no different from all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because they still possess the notion of duality. Consequently, they are unable to abide in the wisdom of the single-flavored activity that experiences integration.

If one has already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one attains a mind of equality by dispelling the two notions; thus, one becomes distinct from Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. By means of this mind of equality, one is able to abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*) and enjoy the unified wisdom of phenomena of a single flavor.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is like various large and small streams that, before entering the great ocean, each have their own separate basis; they consist of different waters, limited waters, and waters that increase or decrease. Depending on the specific functions of those waters, they perform various distinct tasks and provide only a small portion of support for the lives of aquatic creatures."

If one enters the great ocean, there is no separate basis; the water is without distinction, the water is without limit, and the water neither increases nor decreases. Its function is singular: it provides a vast support for the lives of aquatic creatures.

In this way, as long as these bodhisattvas have not yet entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, their respective bases consist of diverse cognitions, limited cognitions, and cognitions that increase or decrease; according to the activities of their respective cognitions, they differ from one another and serve as the basis for maturing the roots of goodness of only a small portion of sentient beings.

If one has already entered the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, there is no other basis; wisdom is undifferentiated, wisdom is immeasurable, and wisdom neither increases nor decreases. One partakes in the unified flavor of the wisdom of phenomena, serving as the locus for the maturation of the roots of goodness of immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The suchness of all phenomena, The characteristic of purity from the two obstacles,
The object-condition for the knowledge of the Dharma, And the characteristic of sovereign inexhaustibility."
The wisdom of universal suchness, cultivated and perfected through practice,
establishes two types of sentient beings; it brings forth various inexhaustible fruits—
the emanations of body, speech, and mind— through the skillful activities of excellent transformation.
The gates of meditative concentration and dhāraṇī, The two infinite accomplishments,
And the transformations of the self-nature, enjoyment, and emanation bodies—
Such is the pure dharma-realm, As taught by all the Buddhas.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Subhūti, along with the great śrāvakas, the devas, humans, asuras, and all the other members of the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted, upheld, and practiced it.
The Sūtra on the Buddha Grounds Spoken by the Buddha
